_metadata.rubric: x01 expansion rubric (owner style examples, clicks-when-explained bar, explanation checked), 2026-10-18
_metadata.independence: I read only x01-a-review-input.json; no other file, repository search, web lookup or paid API was used.

hints.reason: FRANKENSTEIN via the iconic "It's alive!" line; LIGHTNING via the storm bolt that brings the creature to life in that same scene.

best_available.why: One famous movie moment covers both words, and the explanation is accurate (Henry Frankenstein shouts it in the 1931 film).

pairs.pair_note: Clean pair; nothing to repair.

hints.reason: CAR because McQueen is the race car star of Pixar's Cars; LIGHTNING through his full name, Lightning McQueen.

best_available.why: A character name that completes one target and is literally the other.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; LIGHTNING is the name half, CAR the character's nature.

hints.reason: POKEMON as its best-known character and mascot; YELLOW as Pikachu's famous colour (and even the Pokemon Yellow game).

best_available.why: The obvious and fair answer; a little direct but solid.

pairs.pair_note: Direct rather than surprising, but exactly the natural clue in the BARNEY mould.

hints.reason: FLY because flies buzz; SPACE via Buzz Lightyear the space ranger (and Buzz Aldrin as a bonus).

best_available.why: A neat double meaning, a sound for one target and a name for the other.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent double-meaning hint.

hints.reason: COWBOY because Woody is a cowboy doll; TOY via Toy Story and his being a toy; the pull-string quote is accurate.

best_available.why: Woody is, literally, a cowboy toy.

pairs.pair_note: Clean.

hints.reason: CAPTAIN through Captain Hook; CROCODILE through the ticking crocodile that ate his hand and keeps chasing him.

best_available.why: Peter Pan's villain and his nemesis in a single word.

pairs.pair_note: Clean; the explanation is accurate to Barrie and Disney.

hints.reason: VAMPIRE because Dracula is the archetypal vampire; HOTEL only through his role running the hotel in Hotel Transylvania, which needs that film in mind.
HOTEL through the film title Hotel Transylvania; VAMPIRE because Transylvania is Dracula's legendary homeland.

best_available.why: It completes a famous title for HOTEL and evokes vampires on its own, so both sides land without leaning on the film.

pairs.pair_note: Both work; TRANSYLVANIA balances the two sides better, while DRACULA leans on VAMPIRE.

hints.reason: SCARECROW as one of Oz's famous travellers; BRAIN as the thing he asks the Wizard of Oz for.
hints.fix: The Scarecrow already lives in Oz, so reword to: "The Scarecrow followed the yellow brick road to ask the Wizard of Oz for a brain."

best_available.why: A short, iconic story link to both words; only the explanation's wording needs a small fix.

pairs.pair_note: The idea is great; the explanation says he 'went all the way to Oz', but he started in Oz and walked to the Emerald City.

hints.reason: BROOM because Quidditch is played on flying broomsticks; HOGWARTS because it is the school's signature sport.
hints.fix: Use U.S. spelling in the explanation: "Hogwarts' favorite sport is played on flying brooms."

best_available.why: Accurate and well known; only the British spelling 'favourite' should change.

pairs.pair_note: Solid, if a bit expected.

hints.reason: SCORPION because scorpions sting; POLICE via Sting, frontman of The Police (and 'sting operation' as a bonus).

best_available.why: Two independent routes reach POLICE (band and sting operation), and the scorpion side is literal.

pairs.pair_note: Excellent; the backup 'police sting' meaning makes it fair even for players who don't know the band.

hints.reason: HOCKEY through the hockey puck; SHAKESPEARE through Puck, the mischievous fairy in A Midsummer Night's Dream.

best_available.why: A real 'oh, nice' double meaning; the Shakespeare side is school-reading level, not niche.

pairs.pair_note: The Shakespeare side is the weaker half for some players, but it clicks fully once explained.

hints.reason: WOMAN completes Wonder Woman; AMAZON because Diana is an Amazon princess of Themyscira.

best_available.why: Turns AMAZON away from the online store toward mythology, a satisfying pivot.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; the hint does not contain WOMAN, it only completes the title.

hints.reason: MINT through 'minty fresh'; PRINCE through The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air.

best_available.why: A playful pairing of an everyday phrase and a famous TV title.

pairs.pair_note: Fresh Prince is from the 1990s but still widely known and was recently rebooted; not dated.

hints.reason: Both EGG and HAM through the title Green Eggs and Ham, where GREEN describes each.
Both words through Dr. Seuss's Green Eggs and Ham; one step more indirect than GREEN, but his best-known book.

best_available.why: The title's own adjective applies to both targets, so it reads as a single word clue.

pairs.pair_note: Both fine; SEUSS is a good alternative where GREEN might collide with colour words on the board.

hints.reason: CHOCOLATE through Wonka's chocolate factory and bars; TICKET through the golden tickets hidden in them.

best_available.why: The golden ticket in a Wonka bar ties both words to one famous story beat.

pairs.pair_note: Clean.

hints.reason: CHARM via Lucky Charms (and 'lucky charm'); LEPRECHAUN via Lucky the Leprechaun mascot and leprechaun luck folklore.

best_available.why: Phrase, brand and mascot all point to the same pair.

pairs.pair_note: Strong, with several routes.

hints.reason: SENSE through 'sixth sense' / The Sixth Sense; DEAD through the film's famous 'I see dead people' line.

best_available.why: Completes a phrase for one side and evokes an iconic quote for the other.

pairs.pair_note: 1999 film, but the line is still part of pop culture; PG enough as a reference.

hints.reason: DOCTOR through Dr. Jekyll; HIDE as a homophone of Mr. Hyde, his alter ego.

best_available.why: A satisfying homophone pun on a household-name story.

pairs.pair_note: Great pun pair; the explanation openly flags the pun.

hints.reason: STAIRS through the famous 'Rocky Steps' training run; MUSEUM because those are the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

best_available.why: One iconic movie scene contains both targets; a real 'oh, nice' moment.

pairs.pair_note: The MUSEUM side is the less-known half, but it lands as soon as it is explained.

hints.reason: EXPLORE via the explorer Marco Polo; POOL via water polo and the 'Marco... Polo!' pool game.
hints.fix: Mention the pool game, the stronger pool route: "Marco Polo the explorer, and the 'Polo!' every kid shouts back in the pool."

hints.reason: EXPLORE via Marco Polo the explorer; POOL via the 'Marco!' call in the classic pool game.

best_available.why: Two pool routes (water polo and the game) plus the explorer; slightly sturdier than MARCO.

pairs.pair_note: Both halves of the same name work; serve one, not both.

hints.reason: ALIEN because Lilo's companion Stitch is a blue alien; STITCHES through the name Stitch in Lilo & Stitch, a name-to-word pun.

best_available.why: Players complete 'Lilo & Stitch' and the alien follows; fun once seen.

pairs.pair_note: The STITCHES side relies on Stitch the name matching the plural common noun, but that is the kind of pun the owner welcomes; the 2025 live-action remake keeps it current.

hints.reason: BARBIE via Malibu Barbie and her Malibu Dreamhouse; BEACH because Malibu is a famous California beach town.

best_available.why: A place name that belongs to both the doll and the beach.

pairs.pair_note: Clean.

hints.reason: GHOST because Casper is a cartoon ghost; FRIEND through his title 'Casper the Friendly Ghost'.
hints.fix: Lead with the title that carries the FRIEND link: "Casper the Friendly Ghost just wants to make a friend."

best_available.why: His full title nearly spells out both targets.

pairs.pair_note: The idea is perfect; the explanation should name 'the Friendly Ghost', which is the real FRIEND route.

hints.reason: SHOE via the Nike sneaker brand; VICTORY because the brand is named for Nike, Greek goddess of victory.

best_available.why: A brand most know, plus a myth fact many enjoy learning; a real 'oh, nice' moment.

pairs.pair_note: The VICTORY side is trivia, but it is accurate and widely repeated, so it clicks when explained.

hints.reason: PUMPKIN because the Fairy Godmother turns a pumpkin into a coach; CINDERELLA because it carries her to the ball.
CINDERELLA through the midnight deadline; PUMPKIN only through the coach turning back into one at midnight, one step removed.

best_available.why: It is literally the transformed pumpkin, so both sides are equally strong.

pairs.pair_note: COACH is the better-balanced hint; MIDNIGHT leans toward CINDERELLA.

hints.reason: BANANA via the banana peel; SLIP via the classic slapstick gag of slipping on one.

best_available.why: The natural clue: the object at the heart of the gag.

pairs.pair_note: Direct and fair.

hints.reason: PUMPKIN and SPICE together through the pumpkin spice latte, the famous fall drink.

best_available.why: Completes a three-word phrase that everyone knows.

pairs.pair_note: It links the two words as one phrase rather than separately, but the phrase is so familiar that it is fully fair.

hints.reason: DEVIL via the Tasmanian devil (and Looney Tunes' Taz); AUSTRALIA because Tasmania is an Australian island state.

best_available.why: Geography and a famous animal in one word; facts are correct.

pairs.pair_note: Clean.

hints.reason: CAMERA via 'say cheese' for photos; MOUSE via the cartoon mouse-loves-cheese trope.

best_available.why: Two unrelated idioms meet in one word; the explanation sensibly says 'cartoon mice' rather than claim a biological fact.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; the explanation avoids the wrong_fact trap.

hints.reason: BREAKFAST as a breakfast cereal; CHAMPION via its slogan 'The Breakfast of Champions' and athletes on the box.

best_available.why: A brand slogan that contains both targets.

pairs.pair_note: U.S.-specific but well known to a U.S. audience; slightly less familiar to younger players.

hints.reason: NEEDLE via the eye of a needle; POTATO via potato eyes.

best_available.why: A tidy double meaning on two everyday objects.

pairs.pair_note: Clean and satisfying.

hints.reason: SNOWMAN completes 'Abominable Snowman'; HIMALAYAS as the legend's home.
HIMALAYAS as the yeti's legendary home; SNOWMAN only through the yeti's other name, the Abominable Snowman.

best_available.why: Completes the exact phrase containing SNOWMAN while pointing to the Himalayan legend.

pairs.pair_note: ABOMINABLE is the stronger, more surprising route; YETI leans on HIMALAYAS.

hints.reason: Both BIRD and WORM through the proverb 'The early bird catches the worm'.

best_available.why: The proverb holds both targets; the natural clue.

pairs.pair_note: Clean.

hints.reason: FENCE via the fencing sword called a foil; KITCHEN via aluminum foil.

best_available.why: A double meaning that also pushes FENCE from yard to sport; a real 'oh, nice'.

pairs.pair_note: Strong; it takes a reinterpretation of FENCE as the sport, but fencing is broadly known.

hints.reason: FOOT because a standard ruler is one foot (12 inches) long; KING because a king is a ruler.

best_available.why: A crisp double meaning with both sides exact.

pairs.pair_note: Clean; the explanation is accurate.
